prompt: When I got home, my boyfriend and I got into an argument. He got upset and he started hitting his face. That is the first time he has ever done that, but I would be lying if I said that didn't scare me. I locked myself in the room.
response_text:
That must have been really frightening to witness, and it makes complete sense that you felt scared and needed to protect yourself by stepping away. Your instinct to create space when something feels unsafe is valid—please don't doubt that.

When someone hurts themselves during a conflict, it can leave you feeling responsible, confused, or even afraid to speak up. But his actions are not something you caused, and it's important that your safety and wellbeing matter here too. If this behavior continues or escalates, consider reaching out to someone you trust or a professional who can help you both. If you ever feel in immediate danger, don't hesitate to contact emergency services or a domestic support line. You deserve a relationship where you feel safe, not scared—take care of yourself first.

prompt: I been having anger problems a lot lately. It only takes one word wrongly said to set me off. I use to not be like this until I got with my soon-to-be husband. I think his mood and rage/anger problems have rubbed off on me a lot. I don't get nearly as bad as he does, but I yell almost constantly and I can't seem to just stop. I have two young babies that have to hear this, and I don't want my girls growing up with a mommy like I have been lately. I just don't know how to get back to my old self.
response_text:
It takes real courage to notice this pattern and to care so deeply about the kind of mother your daughters experience. The fact that you're aware and want to change is genuinely meaningful.

You mentioned this started after being with your partner, whose rage you're now absorbing. That's worth paying attention to. Living around constant anger can put your nervous system on high alert, making you quicker to snap even when you don't want to. This isn't a personal failing—it's a response to your environment. It may help to think about whether that environment feels safe and how his anger affects you, too.

For the immediate moments, try noticing your early warning signs and giving yourself permission to step away for a minute before reacting. Even a few deep breaths can create space. And please consider reaching out to a counselor who can support you individually. You deserve that help, and your girls will benefit from a mom who's getting supported, not just holding it all alone.

prompt: My issue isn't resisting angry urges; it's the anger itself. My rage is extreme and vastly disproportionate to the direct stressor. It causes violent thoughts, but I never act. I stay lucid enough to know the rage is violent, not me. I don't want to drown myself in anger and resentment.
response_text:
It sounds like you've developed real insight here—you can feel the rage burning intensely while still holding onto the awareness that it doesn't define you, and that you don't want to be consumed by it. That distinction between the anger and yourself is genuinely important, and it's a sign of self-awareness many people struggle to reach.

When emotions feel this disproportionate to what triggered them, it often points to something underneath—old wounds, unmet needs, or feelings that never had a safe place to go. The anger may be carrying more than just the present moment. It might help to explore that with a therapist trained in emotion processing (approaches like EFT or trauma-informed therapy can be useful). In the moment, grounding your body—cold water, hard exercise, slow breathing—can discharge some of the physical intensity so you're not left holding it alone. You're clearly working hard to stay in control and not lose yourself; that effort deserves support, not just willpower.

prompt: When I see something I don’t like, I go off like a ticking time bomb. I go from “0 to 100” really quickly.
response_text:
It takes real self-awareness to recognize this pattern, and naming it is genuinely the first step toward changing it. That "0 to 100" feeling usually means your body is reacting faster than your thinking brain can catch up—your nervous system is hitting the alarm before you've had a chance to decide how to respond.

One thing that can help is learning to notice the earliest physical signs before you hit 100—a tight jaw, heat in your chest, clenched hands. Those are your early warning signals, and catching them gives you a window to pause, breathe, or step away before things escalate.

I'd also gently encourage you to get curious about what's underneath the anger. Often it's protecting something more vulnerable—feeling disrespected, powerless, or unheard. If this is affecting your relationships or how you feel about yourself, talking with a therapist could help you find the root and build lasting tools. You don't have to be at the mercy of these reactions.

prompt: I'm being emotionally abused by my dad. I need advice on how to hold my temper with him
response_text:
I'm really sorry you're dealing with this. It takes a lot of strength to recognize what's happening and to want to protect your own peace, even in such a painful situation.

When you feel your temper rising, try to pause and breathe slowly before responding—even a few seconds can help you stay grounded. You might quietly remind yourself that his words reflect him, not your worth, and that staying calm is a way of protecting yourself, not giving in. If a conversation gets too heated, it's okay to step away by saying you need a moment, then physically leaving the room if you can.

That said, holding your temper shouldn't mean carrying this alone. Emotional abuse is serious, and you deserve support beyond just managing your reactions. Is there a trusted adult, counselor, or friend you could talk to? If you ever feel unsafe, please reach out to a helpline in your area. You matter, and your feelings are valid.

prompt: I start counseling/therapy in a few days (I'm freaking out) but my main fear is that I'll cry and embarrass myself, is it something to worry about?
response_text:
It's completely understandable to feel nervous before your first session—so many people do. But I want to gently reassure you: crying in therapy isn't embarrassing at all. In fact, it's one of the most common and natural things that happens there. Therapists see tears regularly, and it often means you're touching on something that truly matters to you. A good therapist will meet those moments with warmth and patience, never judgment.

Try to think of the therapy room as a space where you don't have to hold anything together or perform. Whatever comes up—tears, silence, messy thoughts—is welcome. You're allowed to just be yourself there. The courage it took to even schedule this appointment says a lot about your strength. Be kind to yourself in these next few days, and know that whatever happens, you're doing something brave and worthwhile.

prompt: I've gone to a couple therapy sessions so far and still everytime I walk in I get nervous and shaky. Is this normal? Should I still be feeling like this?
response_text:
Yes, this is completely normal, and it's actually a really common experience in the early stages of therapy. Opening up to someone—even a professional—can feel vulnerable and unfamiliar, and your nervous system takes time to learn that this is a safe space. A few sessions in, you're still building trust and getting comfortable, so those nerves make a lot of sense.

For many people, that shakiness eases as the relationship with their therapist deepens over time. In the meantime, it might help to mention this to your therapist directly—they've almost certainly heard it before and can help you feel more at ease. Naming the nervousness out loud can actually take some of its power away. Be patient with yourself; showing up despite feeling anxious takes real courage.

prompt: I have been with my boyfriend for more than a year. He recently got a new job and travels a lot. I’m not used to him being gone all the time. I feel as though he has forgotten about me because he does not talk with me as much and doesn’t keep me up to date on everything that he does throughout the day, which he used to. I feel lost, sad and unwanted. This is really a tough new challenge. I just want to break up with him, but I love him so much. I don’t know why he is acting this way lately. I believe I have separation anxiety. Is there anything that I can do to help me cope with this while he is out of town?
response_text:
It makes complete sense that this transition feels hard. You went from constant connection to a new rhythm you didn't choose, and that shift can genuinely trigger feelings of loss and insecurity. Wanting to break up but loving him deeply often signals that you're overwhelmed, not that the relationship is wrong for you.

A few things might help. Try to have an honest, calm conversation with him about what you're feeling and what you need—maybe a set check-in time each day so you both know when to expect contact. It also helps to gently fill your own time with things that ground you: friends, hobbies, movement, or routines that remind you that you're whole on your own, too. His reduced contact may reflect exhaustion or adjustment rather than fading feelings, but you deserve to know for sure. If the anxiety feels persistent or hard to manage, talking with a counselor could give you tools to feel steadier. You're not being needy—you're adjusting to something real.

prompt: I had a head injury a few years ago and my mind races all the time. I have trouble sleeping and have a lot of anxiety. Every medicine I have been on my body rejects; I get sick to my stomach and get blisters in my mouth. How can I calm my self down? I'm a wreck.
response_text:
I'm really sorry you're dealing with this—it sounds exhausting to have your mind racing constantly while also struggling to find medication your body can tolerate. That combination would leave anyone feeling like a wreck, so please be gentle with yourself.

Since medications have been so hard on you, it may help to lean on non-medication tools. Slow breathing can genuinely calm your nervous system—try breathing in for four counts, holding for four, and exhaling for six, repeating for a few minutes. Grounding techniques, gentle movement like walking, and limiting screens before bed can also ease a racing mind. Given your head injury, I'd strongly encourage checking in with a neurologist or doctor who can look at how the injury may be affecting your sleep and anxiety, since that specialized support matters here.

You're clearly trying hard to help yourself, and that takes strength. Please don't go through this alone—reaching out to a professional could make a real difference.

prompt: I think I'm annoying and bothersome, but my girlfriend says I'm just fine. I don't think so, I think I'm stressing everyone else out
response_text:
It sounds like there's a real gap between how you see yourself and how the people close to you actually experience you. That kind of self-doubt can be exhausting—constantly worrying that you're too much for others, even when they're telling you otherwise.

It might help to gently ask yourself where this belief comes from. Often these feelings aren't really about the present moment but grow from older experiences of feeling rejected or like a burden. Your girlfriend knows you and is choosing to be with you, so her reassurance is worth taking seriously, even when it's hard to believe. If this worry keeps weighing on you or affecting your relationships, talking with a therapist could help you understand and soften that inner critic. You deserve to feel at ease being yourself around the people who care about you.

prompt: How can I control my anxiety when I have Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder?
response_text:
Managing anxiety with OCD can feel exhausting, and I want you to know that what you're experiencing is real and treatable. One of the most effective approaches is learning to sit with the discomfort of anxious thoughts without responding to them through compulsions. This is hard at first, but each time you resist the urge to "neutralize" a thought, you teach your brain that the anxiety will pass on its own. Grounding techniques—like slow breathing or naming things you can see and hear—can also help you ride out the intensity in the moment.

That said, OCD often responds best to specialized support, particularly a therapy called Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP), which is considered the gold standard. If you haven't already, connecting with a therapist trained in OCD can make a meaningful difference, and medication is an option worth discussing too. You're not alone in this, and with the right tools, things can genuinely improve. Be gentle with yourself along the way.

prompt: I am extremely possessive in my relationships and this is hurting my friendships. How can I fix my underlying issues?
response_text:
It takes real self-awareness to recognize this pattern and want to change it—that's genuinely a strong first step.

Possessiveness often grows from deeper fears: fear of abandonment, insecurity, or past experiences where people we trusted let us down. When you feel that grip of jealousy or the urge to control, try pausing to ask yourself what you're actually afraid of losing, and whether that fear matches reality. Building your own sense of security—through hobbies, self-worth, and a life that feels full outside your relationships—can loosen that need to hold on so tightly.

It's also worth being honest with the friends you trust; letting them know you're working on this can ease the pressure on both sides. If these patterns feel deeply rooted or hard to shift alone, working with a therapist can help you explore where they come from and build healthier ways of connecting. You're clearly capable of growth—be patient with yourself as you practice.

prompt: I start to think of an issue that doesn't even matter or something bad that happened years ago. Then, I cry, pull at my hair, plug my ears, hit myself, and throw things. In loud public places, I get on edge and start being sarcastic and moody. I have an awful fear of people leaving me (which normally ends up happening) and I feel like I'm too clingy.
response_text:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot of pain, and those moments when your mind pulls you back to old hurts can feel overwhelming and exhausting. The intensity of what you're describing—the crying, hitting yourself, the sensitivity to noise, the deep fear of being left—suggests your nervous system is often in a state of distress, and that's genuinely hard to live with. Please know that none of this makes you "too much" or broken.

These patterns—emotional intensity, fear of abandonment, self-directed anger—are things that can improve a lot with the right support, especially with a therapist trained in approaches like DBT, which helps with emotional regulation and relationships. I'd really encourage you to reach out to a mental health professional, and if you ever feel unsafe with the self-hitting, please contact a crisis line right away.

You deserve care and steadiness, not fear. Being clingy often comes from a real wound, not a flaw—and it can heal. You're not alone in this.

prompt: I am lazy. I am very aware of the problem and try to talk myself out of it all the time, but I never seem to shake the habits. I try to think of what it is doing to me and my future, but no matter what, I keep creating excuses for myself to continue the procrastination. All I'm ever left with is regrets and a low grade. I am at an all-time low in my life, and I'm not even that old. I've always been a straight-A student, but now I'm getting C's and F's, and it hurts me to know that I am way better than that. It's not even like the work is hard.
response_text:
What you're describing doesn't sound like laziness to me—it sounds like something heavier. When a straight-A student suddenly can't get themselves to do work that isn't even hard, that's often a sign of something deeper: burnout, depression, anxiety, or exhaustion that no amount of willpower can just push through. Truly lazy people don't lie awake feeling this much pain about it. You clearly care a lot, which is why this hurts so much.

Please try to be gentler with yourself. Calling yourself lazy and pushing harder hasn't worked, and it may actually be adding shame that makes it harder to move. Consider talking to a doctor or counselor about what you're feeling—especially since you mention being at an all-time low. And if you can, start impossibly small: not "do the whole assignment," but "open the document for two minutes." Momentum often follows action, not motivation. You're not broken, and this doesn't have to be permanent.

prompt: I never get infections or scars or anything, and it doesn't bother me if it gets filled up with blood or something, but I'm concerned.
response_text:
It sounds like something has been happening physically that's worrying you, but I'm missing some context about what specifically is concerning you. Are you referring to injuries, wounds, or something you're doing to yourself intentionally?

I want to make sure I understand before offering support. If you're experiencing thoughts of harming yourself, or if this involves self-injury, please know that's something worth talking through with someone who can really help—whether that's a therapist, doctor, or a crisis line like 988 (Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, call or text) if you're in the US.

Even if injuries heal cleanly without scars or infections, the fact that you feel "concerned" matters. That concern is worth listening to. Could you share a bit more about what's going on? You deserve support, and reaching out is a meaningful first step.

prompt: How do you know you have the right therapist for you? How would I know how to "train" my therapist to be able to give me what I need from treatment?
response_text:
Great questions—and the fact that you're thinking about this shows real self-awareness about your care.

A good fit often feels like this: you sense your therapist listens without judgment, you gradually feel safe being honest, and you notice their approach seems to help you move forward, even if the work is hard. It's normal for it to take a few sessions to settle in, but you shouldn't feel consistently dismissed or misunderstood.

As for "training" them—you don't have to figure it out alone. A good therapist welcomes your feedback. You can say things like, "I tend to need more structure," or "When you do X, it helps me," or "I didn't find that last approach useful—can we try something different?" Naming what you need is actually part of the therapeutic process, and it teaches them how to work with *you* specifically.

If you've tried voicing your needs and still feel unheard, that's useful information too—it may mean this isn't the right match, and that's okay.

prompt: Does counseling really do anything that can help people?
response_text:
That's a fair question to ask, especially if you're considering whether it's worth your time and energy.

Honestly, counseling isn't magic, and it doesn't work the same for everyone. But for many people, it helps in a few key ways: having someone listen without judgment, gaining tools to manage difficult emotions, and understanding patterns you might not see on your own. Research does show it can be effective for a wide range of struggles, though a lot depends on the fit between you and the therapist, and your willingness to engage.

If you've had a bad experience before, or you're just skeptical, that's understandable. It's okay to try it and decide it's not for you, or to look for a different therapist if the first one doesn't click. You don't have to commit forever to give it a fair shot. What matters most is that you're wondering how to feel better, and that's a genuinely good starting point.

prompt: How does a person start the counseling process?
response_text:
Starting counseling is a meaningful step, and it's understandable to feel unsure about how to begin. A good first move is to check whether your health insurance covers mental health services, as this can help narrow your options. If you don't have insurance or prefer other routes, many communities offer sliding-scale clinics, and your primary care doctor can often provide referrals. Online directories like Psychology Today let you filter therapists by location, specialty, and cost.

When you reach out to a counselor, it's okay to ask about their experience, approach, and fees before committing. Many offer a brief consultation to see if it feels like a good fit. Finding the right match sometimes takes a couple of tries, and that's completely normal. The most important thing is simply taking that first contact, whether by phone, email, or an online form. You've already shown courage by asking this question, and that same willingness will carry you forward.

prompt: What are the basic skills a good counselor needs to have?
response_text:
A good counselor relies on a few core skills. At the heart is active listening—truly hearing what someone says without judgment, and reflecting it back so they feel understood. Empathy is essential too: the ability to genuinely connect with another person's experience while maintaining appropriate boundaries. Strong communication, including asking open-ended questions and knowing when to stay silent, helps clients explore their own thoughts.

Beyond these, counselors need self-awareness to recognize their own biases and reactions, cultural sensitivity to work respectfully with diverse people, and patience, since growth takes time. Ethical judgment and confidentiality build the trust that makes therapy possible. Finally, the ability to sit with difficult emotions—without rushing to fix everything—allows clients to feel safe.

If you're considering this path, know that many of these skills can be learned and strengthened over time through training, supervision, and practice. It's a meaningful field, and your interest in doing it well is already a good sign.

prompt: What are some difficulties that a counselor can encounter when dealing with a client?
response_text:
Counselors face many challenges in their work. One common difficulty is building rapport, especially with clients who are guarded, resistant, or mandated to attend. It can take time and patience to establish trust, and progress may feel slow. Managing your own emotional reactions—known as countertransference—can also be tricky, particularly when a client's story resonates with your own experiences.

Other challenges include navigating clients in crisis or with risk of self-harm, working within cultural or value differences, and managing your own burnout or compassion fatigue over time. Ethical dilemmas, such as confidentiality limits or dual relationships, can also arise. Finally, it can be hard to accept that you can't "fix" everyone; some clients disengage or don't improve as hoped, which requires managing your own expectations.

Regular supervision, ongoing training, and good self-care are essential for working through these difficulties effectively. If you're a student or new counselor, know that these challenges are normal and part of professional growth.

prompt: My last relationships have ended horribly. They just up and abandoned me. One of them I have never gotten closure with over it, leaving me emotionally wrecked. I know something's wrong with me but I don't know how to even start trying to better myself. I get into these depressed like states whenever anyone I care about is too busy to be with me. I know that I shouldn't act like that because people are genuinely busy, but I feel like they're doing it just because they don't want to be around me.
response_text:
It takes real courage to look honestly at these patterns, and the fact that you're asking how to grow says a lot about your capacity for change. What you're describing—the fear of abandonment, reading someone's busyness as rejection, sinking into those low states—these are understandable responses, often rooted in past experiences where people really did leave. It doesn't mean something is "wrong" with you; it means you were hurt and your mind is trying to protect you.

The lack of closure you mentioned can leave a wound that keeps reopening. Working with a therapist could help you process that loss and learn to soothe yourself when those anxious feelings hit, rather than assuming the worst. In the meantime, when you notice that spiral starting, try gently asking yourself: "Is there actual evidence they're avoiding me, or is this an old fear talking?" That small pause can create space between feeling and reaction. You're not broken—you're someone learning to heal, and that's absolutely possible.

prompt: I just feel sad all the time and I don't like anyone in my family. I feel like they're trying to control me and won't let me grow.
response_text:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now—both the heaviness of feeling sad so consistently, and the frustration of feeling controlled by the people around you. That combination can be really exhausting, especially when the people you'd normally lean on feel like part of the problem.

I want to gently name that feeling sad "all the time" is worth paying attention to—it may be more than just family stress, and you deserve support for that too. When it comes to your family, it can help to get specific: what does "growing" look like for you, and where do you feel most held back? Sometimes what feels like control is a clash over independence, and finding small, concrete areas to assert yourself can make a difference. If it feels safe, talking to a counselor—even one at school—could give you space to sort through both the sadness and the family tension. You don't have to figure this out alone.

prompt: I self-harm, and I stop for awhile. Then when I see something sad or depressing, I automatically want to self-harm.
response_text:
It takes real strength to notice this pattern in yourself, and the fact that you've been able to stop for periods shows you're capable of getting through those urges. What you're describing—being triggered by sad or upsetting things—is something a lot of people who self-harm experience, and it doesn't mean you're failing or back at square one.

When that automatic urge hits, it can help to have a plan ready before the moment comes. Some people use ice, intense exercise, drawing on their skin, or reaching out to someone until the wave passes. It also might help to gently limit or step back from the content that tends to set you off, at least while you're building other coping tools.

If you haven't already, please consider talking to a therapist who can help you understand your triggers and build safer responses. You deserve that support, and you don't have to manage this alone.

prompt: I'm depressed. I have been for years. I hide it from everyone because I'm scared of the reactions I'll get. Last time I tried telling my parents, it was a huge argument about me being too young to be depressed (I’m a legal adult), calling me ungrateful, and telling me that if I can't handle things now, it's only going to get worse in the future (which is turning out to be true). It's exhausting pretending to be okay, and I don't know how much longer I can try. I'm just really tired, and sadly, I can't afford the help I need on my own.
response_text:
I'm really glad you reached out here, and I want you to know that what you're carrying sounds incredibly heavy. Pretending to be okay for years is exhausting in a way most people can't imagine, and the fact that you've kept going says a lot about your strength, even when you feel depleted.

Your parents' reaction wasn't fair, and it wasn't a reflection of whether your pain is real. Depression doesn't have an age limit, and you deserve support regardless of what anyone else says. When you mention being "really tired" and not knowing how much longer you can try, I want to check in gently—if you're having thoughts of not being here, please reach out to a crisis line like 988 (call or text, US) where someone can talk with you right now, for free.

There are low-cost options too: sliding-scale therapists, community mental health centers, and warmlines. You don't have to keep holding this alone. Would you be open to trying one of these?

prompt: He said he would try and he never did. It's been nine months, and this is making me worse. Today, he said I have to respect whatever decision he makes. Is that true? Am I supposed to respect the decision to leave because he can't handle what I'm going through and leaves me here crying and worried every night? He's constantly changing his mind on if he wants to work it out.
response_text:
It makes complete sense that you're exhausted and hurting. Nine months of uncertainty, of someone saying they'll try and then not following through, of changing their mind again and again—that's incredibly painful. You're not wrong for feeling worse. Living in that kind of limbo, crying and worried every night, would wear anyone down.

Here's the thing about "respecting his decision": you can accept that he's allowed to make his own choices while also recognizing that some of those choices hurt you deeply. Respecting his right to decide doesn't mean you have to keep waiting, keep absorbing the back-and-forth, or keep sacrificing your own peace. You deserve stability and honesty too.

It might help to ask yourself what *you* need right now, separate from what he decides. What would it look like to protect your own wellbeing? You matter in this, and your feelings are valid. If you can, please consider leaning on a friend or a therapist for support—you shouldn't have to carry this alone.

prompt: Every time my partner gets angry for anything, she takes it out on me. Nothing I do is right, and once she's mad, she calls me all kinds of names and is verbally abusive. She says it isn’t abuse, it’s just angry verbal bashing, and that it’s different. It gets worse each time. The names are very vulgar now.
response_text:
What you're describing is verbal abuse, regardless of what it's called. When someone repeatedly attacks you with vulgar names and makes you feel like nothing you do is right, that's harmful—and the fact that it's escalating is a serious concern. Renaming it "angry verbal bashing" doesn't change its impact on you.

You deserve to feel safe and respected in your relationship. It might help to notice how you feel after these episodes—anxious, small, walking on eggshells? Those feelings matter. Please consider reaching out to a counselor who can support you individually, and if it ever feels unsafe, a domestic abuse hotline can offer guidance confidentially. You're not overreacting, and you don't have to carry this alone.

prompt: My friend’s husband is bipolar and refuses to take medication for it. He has taken the wheels off her vehicle before to prevent her from leaving. He has held her a prisoner in her home. He has choked her, hit her, etc. She has almost divorced him a couple of times but always makes up with him, thinking that he is going to change. She and I went to a wedding out of town in September of 2014, and ever since she has been back, he is convinced that she cheated on him while we were gone. Now he is saying that I have also cheated on my boyfriend and has come to my house and told my boyfriend this.
response_text:
This sounds incredibly stressful, and I can hear how much you care about your friend while also feeling the impact of his behavior on your own life. What you're describing—him physically harming her, imprisoning her, and now spreading accusations that reach into your relationship—is serious. This is domestic abuse, not just bipolar disorder, and the two shouldn't be confused.

The hardest truth is that you can't force your friend to leave, no matter how much you want to protect her. What you can do is stay a steady, nonjudgmental presence so she knows she has somewhere to turn when she's ready. You might gently share the National Domestic Violence Hotline (1-800-799-7233) with her.

Meanwhile, please protect yourself too. His coming to your home to make accusations is a boundary violation. Talk openly with your boyfriend, and consider limiting direct contact with him. If you feel unsafe, documenting incidents or seeking your own support isn't overreacting—it's wise. You matter in this too.

prompt: After a domestic abuse situation, I went to a therapist, and then my husband went. The therapist discussed her assessment of borderline personality disorder with me. She then told my abuser the results of my tests.
response_text:
I'm so sorry this happened to you. What you're describing is a serious breach of therapeutic ethics and confidentiality. A therapist sharing your assessment results with anyone—especially the person who abused you—without your explicit consent is a violation of professional standards, and it may have put your safety at further risk. Please know that this was not your fault, and your feelings of betrayal are completely valid.

You have options here. You can file a complaint with your state's licensing board, which oversees therapist conduct. It may also help to find a new therapist—ideally one experienced in trauma and domestic abuse—who can support you in a safe, confidential space and help you process both the abuse and this breach of trust.

Your safety matters most right now. If you ever feel in danger, the National Domestic Violence Hotline (1-800-799-7233) is available 24/7. You deserve care that protects and respects you.

prompt: I've been with my boyfriend over 3 years. He cheated on me and the woman is now pregnant. He is physically and mentally abusive towards me. I have attempted to talk with him in order to resolve our issues; however, he never wants to talk and often blames me for everything. I’m always there when he needs my help. He tells me although I help him doesn’t mean that I am a good person. He always discredits me as a woman and it’s hurtful. I spend most day crying and feeling lonely. I am unhappy and unsure of what I need to do.
response_text:
I'm so sorry you're carrying this much pain. What you're describing—physical and emotional abuse, betrayal, constant blame, being made to feel worthless—is not something you caused, and it's not something you deserve. The fact that you're crying most days and feeling this lonely tells me how deeply this is hurting you, and I want you to know your feelings are completely valid.

I want to gently say this: abuse rarely improves through talking, especially when he refuses to take responsibility. You've been trying so hard to fix something that isn't yours to fix. Please consider reaching out to a domestic violence hotline—they can offer confidential support and help you think through your safety, with no pressure to make any decision right away.

You matter, and you deserve to feel safe and respected. You don't have to figure this all out at once. Could you reach out to one trusted person this week—a friend, family member, or hotline—just so you're not carrying this alone?

prompt: Now I have anger and trust issues. How can I treat this and fix myself?
response_text:
It takes real courage to recognize these patterns and want to work on them—that self-awareness is already a meaningful first step.

I want to gently offer a reframe: you're not broken and don't need "fixing." Anger and trust issues usually develop for understandable reasons, often as protection after being hurt. Healing tends to come from understanding where these feelings come from, not fighting against yourself.

prompt: Can a past therapist disclose information to a current therapist that you are seeing?
response_text:
That's a really important question, and it's good that you're thinking about your privacy.

Generally, no—a past therapist cannot share your information with a current therapist without your written consent. Therapist-client confidentiality is protected by laws like HIPAA (in the U.S.) and professional ethics codes. If your therapists want to communicate about your care, they typically need you to sign a release of information form authorizing that specific exchange.

There are limited exceptions, such as situations involving imminent risk of harm to yourself or others, suspected abuse, or a court order—but routine sharing between providers requires your permission.

If you'd like your therapists to coordinate care, you can request a release form; if you'd prefer they don't communicate, you're within your rights to decline. It might help to ask your current therapist directly about their confidentiality policies so you feel clear and comfortable. You deserve to have control over who accesses your personal information.

prompt: Can a counselor take sides with one parent and allow a parent to order the child to tell the counselor "every detail" about what happened during the other parent’s visitation in order to help build a case for child custody?

If you believe this is happening, you have options: you can raise your concerns directly with the counselor, request a different provider, or file a complaint with the therapist's state licensing board. If custody proceedings are underway, it's worth mentioning this to your attorney or the court, as inappropriate therapist conduct can be relevant.

Your instinct to question this is reasonable. Protecting the child from being caught in the middle matters most here.

prompt: I have four children. One of them is in her 20s, and she cannot afford to go, nor can I pay for her. She went last year for two weeks by herself.
response_text:
It sounds like you're carrying some worry or guilt about this situation—maybe feeling caught between wanting to give your daughter something and the reality of what's financially possible right now.

It's okay to have limits. Being a caring parent doesn't mean you have to fund everything, especially with three other children and your own financial responsibilities to consider. Your daughter is in her twenties and managed a trip on her own last year, which shows she's capable of finding her own way. You can be honest and loving while still saying, "I can't cover this, but I believe you'll figure it out." That honesty is actually a gift.

If you'd like, it might help to reflect on what's driving the pressure you feel—is it her disappointment, comparison to her siblings, or something else? Understanding that can make the decision feel less heavy. You're allowed to make choices that protect your own stability.

prompt: I am divorced and happily remarried. Our blended family of children are in their 20s. My youngest, age 20, continues to call me crazy and favors her dad. He was abusive to me, and I left with injuries. He never wanted kids, and I did. He paid child support only through forced wage earners. Now my daughters favor him after all the sacrifices I made for them the past 15 years as a single mom. I don’t deny them a relationship with their dad, but to be called crazy and then watch them hang out with him hurts me to the very core. I’m not sure how to handle this.
response_text:
I can hear how deeply this wounds you—after years of sacrifice and protecting your children, being called "crazy" and watching them favor the person who hurt you must feel like a betrayal of everything you gave. That pain is completely valid.

One hard truth is that your daughters may not fully understand what you endured, and at 20, they're still forming their own narratives. You don't have to defend yourself or compete for their loyalty. What you can do is calmly name your boundary: "I love you, and I won't accept being called crazy." You're allowed to protect your dignity even while keeping the door open. Their choices about their dad aren't a verdict on your worth as a mother. Consider talking with a therapist to process this grief, so their words hold less power over how you see yourself. You know the truth of what you gave them—and someday, they may too.

prompt: How does a counselor decide when to end counseling sessions or to terminate working with a client?
response_text:
Great question—termination is usually a collaborative decision, not something the counselor decides alone. Ideally, it happens when you've made meaningful progress toward the goals you set together, feel more equipped to handle challenges on your own, and your symptoms or concerns have improved or stabilized. Many counselors will check in periodically about how therapy is going and whether it's still meeting your needs, which opens space to talk about wrapping up or spacing out sessions.

There are also practical or ethical reasons a counselor might refer you elsewhere—for example, if your needs fall outside their area of expertise, if a conflict of interest arises, or if therapy no longer seems beneficial. A good counselor should discuss this openly with you and help with the transition. If you're wondering about ending your own sessions, it's completely appropriate to bring it up directly with your therapist. That conversation itself can be a valuable part of the process.

prompt: My therapist is gay so there are no sexual issues here. However, my therapist for six years has made me believe that he cares about me and that we are friends. I have loaned money to him many times, and he always paid me back. I had a medical emergency last weekend and I was heavily medicated. I knew that this therapist came into my home and wrote down my credit card information so he could pay back what he owed me, but this therapist dropped me off and never came again. I don't know what to do.
response_text:
It sounds like you're feeling confused and hurt, and understandably so. What you're describing raises some serious concerns. A therapist loaning and borrowing money with a client, entering your home, and accessing your credit card information all cross important professional boundaries that exist specifically to protect you. This isn't about whether he's a caring person—it's about a relationship that has become tangled in ways that aren't healthy or appropriate for therapy.

I'd gently encourage you to prioritize your safety here. If you're worried your credit card information may be misused, contact your bank right away to monitor or protect your account. It may also help to document what you remember while it's fresh. You have the right to file a complaint with your state's licensing board if you feel your trust was violated.

You deserve support that's safe and clear. Please consider reaching out to a new therapist who can help you process all of this without any conflict of interest.

prompt: I just wanted to get to know one so I can hear about their college experience and the courses they took. I also wanted to know if they enjoy their job and how long they were in school.
response_text:
It sounds like you're curious about a particular career path and want to hear from someone who's actually walked it—that's a really smart and practical approach to exploring your options.

A few ways to connect with people in the field: LinkedIn is great for reaching out directly, and most professionals are happy to do a brief "informational interview" if you send a polite message explaining you're exploring the career. You can also check if your school has an alumni network, or ask professors, family, or friends if they know anyone in the field. Professional associations and industry meetups (many are free) are another good option.

When you reach out, keep it short and specific—mention you'd love 15-20 minutes to hear about their college experience, coursework, and what they enjoy about the job. Most people appreciate genuine curiosity.

If you let me know which career you're interested in, I'd be glad to help you find the right places to look.

prompt: I am an international student, and it is my first semester in graduate school in the United States. I faced a cultural shock, and I was so depressed when I arrived here. My counselor in the university was my savior. He helped me a great deal. Now I am going back to my country for a vacation. I was thinking to get him something special with my country's name on it, and I remembered that he likes wine. My country is known for that. Is it appropriate to give him wine as a gift after Christmas?
response_text:
It's clear your counselor made a real difference during a difficult transition, and wanting to express gratitude speaks well of you. That said, gifts to therapists and counselors can be a delicate area. Many universities and counseling professions have ethical guidelines that limit or discourage accepting gifts, and alcohol in particular can be complicated—since it's a personal item and its acceptability varies by workplace policy and personal circumstances.

A thoughtful alternative might be a small, symbolic item representing your country, or simply a heartfelt thank-you note or card telling him how much his support meant to you. Often, sincere words mean more to counselors than any physical gift. If you'd still like to give something, you could ask him directly whether he's able to accept a small token—that way you respect any boundaries he may have. Either way, your gratitude itself is a meaningful gift.

prompt: I'm worried I should see a therapist due to past events and current mental status. I'm just so unsure of how to ask my doctor about seeing someone.
response_text:
It's completely understandable to feel unsure about how to bring this up—many people find that first step to be the hardest part. The good news is that doctors have these conversations often, and you don't need perfect words to start.

You could keep it simple and honest, something like: "I've been struggling with some things from my past and how I'm feeling lately, and I think talking to a therapist might help. Can you point me in the right direction?" You don't have to explain everything in detail—just enough to open the door. If saying it out loud feels overwhelming, it's okay to write it down beforehand or even hand your doctor a note.

The fact that you're recognizing you might need support shows real self-awareness and courage. Reaching out is a meaningful step, and you deserve to have that help. I hope you're able to have that conversation soon.

prompt: I'm obsessing about a terrible breakup. Everything is a constant reminder. How do I move on?
response_text:
Breakups can feel all-consuming, and the fact that everything reminds you of them shows how much this relationship mattered to you. That kind of grief is real, and it takes time to move through—there's no shortcut, but there is a way forward.

For now, be gentle with yourself. Try to gradually reduce the reminders you have control over—muting their social media, putting away shared items, changing up routines that trigger the hardest memories. When the obsessive thoughts hit, notice them without judgment and gently redirect your attention to something grounding, even something small like a walk or reaching out to a friend. Healing isn't linear, so some days will be harder than others, and that's okay. If these thoughts start to feel unmanageable or affect your daily functioning, talking to a therapist can really help you process it. You won't feel this way forever, even though it's hard to believe right now.

prompt: I know that I need to get past my feelings for this person I fell in love with, but t's so difficult to move on because he showed me feelings I've never felt before. I feel like I don't want to be without my genuine love for him, but logically, I know I need to be without him. I can't discuss this with anybody in my life because the conditions surrounding our love are considered "wrong" by a lot of people. How can I get myself to just move on?
response_text:
It sounds like you're carrying this heartache mostly alone, and that isolation makes an already painful situation even harder. First, please know that the feelings themselves are valid—love that awakened something new in you leaves a real mark, and grieving that is natural, not weakness.

Moving on rarely happens by force; it happens gradually as you let yourself feel the loss instead of fighting it. You might try writing out everything you can't say aloud—your love, your grief, why you know it needs to end. Getting it out of your head can ease some of that pressure. And even if you can't share the specifics with people in your life, a therapist offers a confidential, judgment-free space where the "conditions" don't have to be hidden.

Be gentle with yourself. You're not choosing logic over love because you don't feel deeply—you're choosing it because you're trying to protect yourself. That's a kind of strength, even when it hurts.

prompt: My wife just last week said she wants a divorce and it's all sudden. I understand that marriages have their ups and downs but I don't understand why she can't tell me why she wants a divorce. Should I fight for my family (daughter and wife)?
response_text:
I can hear how blindsided and hurt you are right now—being told your marriage is ending without a clear reason leaves you grasping for answers, and that's an incredibly painful place to be.

Before deciding whether to "fight," it may help to shift the goal toward understanding. Ask your wife, calmly, if she'd be willing to talk—or even try couples counseling—so you can hear what's really going on. Something this sudden often has a longer story behind it, and she may need to feel safe enough to share it. That said, you can't control her choice, only how you show up. Focus on being steady, especially for your daughter, who needs you grounded no matter what happens.

Fighting for your family looks less like resisting the divorce and more like staying present, honest, and open. Whatever the outcome, please lean on trusted friends or a therapist of your own—you shouldn't carry this alone.

prompt: I keep on begging him to come back. I am so unhappy with him but am so scared of being a single parent to our son. I was abused as a little girl and that has made to be very abusive to men. What should I do...
response_text:
It takes real courage to be this honest about what you're feeling and about the patterns you've noticed in yourself. I hear two things: you're deeply unhappy in this relationship, yet the fear of parenting alone keeps pulling you back. Both of those feelings make complete sense, especially given the abuse you survived as a child. That kind of early trauma often shapes how we connect with others, and it's not a character flaw—it's a wound that deserves care.

Please consider reaching out to a therapist, ideally one who specializes in trauma. Working through what happened to you could ease both the fear and the patterns you're describing, and help you make relationship decisions from a steadier place rather than from panic. You might also look into local single-parent support resources, so that fear feels a little less overwhelming. You don't have to untangle all of this alone—and you deserve support as you figure out what's truly best for you and your son.

prompt: How do couples keep from being at risk for divorce?
response_text:
Great question—and the fact that you're thinking about this shows real intentionality about your relationship.

Research points to a few things that make a meaningful difference. Couples who stay strong tend to prioritize regular, honest communication—especially about the small frustrations before they build up. They handle conflict with respect, avoiding contempt, criticism, and stonewalling, and they repair quickly after arguments. Feeling like teammates rather than opponents matters a lot. So does maintaining friendship and appreciation: noticing what your partner does right, expressing gratitude, and staying curious about each other as you both grow and change.

It also helps to align on core values and big-picture goals like finances, family, and lifestyle, and to keep investing in the relationship rather than taking it for granted.

No couple does this perfectly, and struggling doesn't mean you're headed for divorce. Many couples find that seeing a therapist—together or individually—during good times, not just crises, strengthens their foundation. Would that be something you'd consider exploring?

prompt: We've been in a long distance relationship for two and a half years. I recently saw his phone and saw the people he texts the most and one of them was a female coworker. I don't know how to approach this situation. How do I ask him about it?.
response_text:
It makes sense that seeing this stirred up some worry, especially with the distance already testing your connection. The good news is that a coworker showing up in his frequent texts doesn't automatically mean something is wrong—but your feelings are valid, and this is worth talking through with him.

When you bring it up, try leading with honesty rather than accusation. Something like, "I noticed you text a coworker often, and it brought up some insecurity for me. Can we talk about it?" This opens the door without putting him on the defensive. Pay attention to how he responds—openness and reassurance are good signs, while defensiveness or secrecy may be worth exploring further.

It might also help to gently ask yourself where this worry comes from. Is it about him specifically, or does the distance leave you feeling uncertain in general? Understanding that can guide the conversation and help you both feel more secure moving forward.

prompt: I’ve been in a long distance relationship with my girlfriend for just over a year. This past week she admitted to me that she has feelings for another guy. She says it’s “just a crush” but I don't know how to cope with it. How should I deal with this?
response_text:
I can hear how much this is hurting you, and that makes complete sense. Learning that your partner has feelings for someone else—even if she calls it "just a crush"—can shake your sense of security and leave you questioning where you stand. Those feelings are valid.

It might help to have an honest conversation with her about what this crush means for your relationship and what you both need moving forward. Ask yourself: Does her openness feel like a betrayal, or like her being transparent so you can work through it together? Neither answer is wrong, but knowing how you feel will guide your next step.

Long distance is genuinely hard, and no relationship is immune to attraction to others. What matters is how you both handle it. Give yourself permission to feel unsettled, and don't rush to a decision while emotions are raw. You deserve a relationship where you feel secure and valued—take the time to figure out if this is one.

prompt: However, it seems as though he is really talking to someone other than himself. I have even accused him of having a secret phone. Is he trying to make me crazy on purpose, or is he really talking to himself?
response_text:
It sounds like you're feeling confused and uneasy about what you're observing, and that uncertainty is understandably distressing. When we can't make sense of someone's behavior, our minds often fill in explanations—sometimes reaching for possibilities like hidden phones or intentional manipulation.

Before assuming he's trying to make you feel crazy, it may help to gently share what you've noticed and how it's affecting you, rather than leading with accusations. Something like, "I've noticed you talking, and I'm not sure who to, and it's been worrying me." His response can tell you a lot. There are many possible explanations—thinking out loud, stress, or something worth a doctor's attention if it seems out of character. Trust your instincts, but also give room for honest conversation. If you continue feeling manipulated or anxious in this relationship, speaking with a counselor could help you sort through your feelings and figure out your next steps. You deserve clarity and peace of mind.

prompt: I'm in a relationship with my fiancé and I currently found out that she's been cheating on me with a co-worker. I was very upset none the less. I understand what she did was wrong, but I want to spend the rest of my life with her. So I'm willing to forgive and move on. We have been together for a little over 9 years, and we have a son. At the beginning of our relationship, I was unfaithful and she caught me cheating. She forgave me for what I've done to her and since then I been completely faithful. I'm worried about our relationship and want to move forward but its been very unsettling. All I can think about is her with another man. I don't know what to do or where to go for advice?
response_text:
I can hear how much pain you're carrying right now, and how much this relationship means to you. Betrayal cuts deep, and the fact that you're picturing her with someone else is a completely normal response to that hurt. Wanting to move forward while still feeling unsettled isn't a contradiction—it's part of the process of healing.

Choosing to forgive is meaningful, but forgiveness and rebuilding trust take time and honest conversations, not just a decision to move on. It might help to talk openly with her about what led to this, and what you both need to feel secure again. Given your history together, couples counseling could give you a safe space to work through these feelings and rebuild your foundation. Individual therapy could also help you process the intrusive thoughts you're having. You've both hurt and forgiven each other before—that shows real commitment. With support, you can work toward something stronger. You don't have to figure this out alone.

prompt: We’ve been together almost three years. We argue and he ends it by telling me he doesn’t love me. It's hurtful because I am all about resolving the problem, and he dwells on the issue even if I drop what he's done and just swallow my pride and say I am sorry. How can this be resolved? We have kids, and I don't want a broken family because we can't communicate.
response_text:
It sounds exhausting to keep reaching for repair while he responds by threatening the relationship itself. That kind of "I don't love you" during conflict is deeply wounding, and it makes sense you're worried about your family—and about carrying so much of the emotional labor alone.

One thing worth noticing: staying together "for the kids" only helps them if the home feels emotionally safe. Kids absorb the tension either way. So the real question isn't just how to avoid a broken family, but how to build a healthier one.

I'd gently encourage you two to talk about this when you're both calm, not mid-argument. Try naming what you need: "When you say you don't love me, it scares me and shuts me down." If he's unwilling to work on how he handles conflict, couples counseling could give you both tools—and clarity about whether this is workable. You deserve a partner who fights *for* the relationship, not against it.

prompt: I'm always told I'm not good enough or trying hard enough. I put 100% in to every thing. I'm worn out, I've worked on all of my family relationships, I'm doing great in school, I'm kind to those in need and otherwise. I stick to my religious beliefs and leave room for mistakes and learn from others so I don't have to make as many and the ones I do I learn from. Somehow it's still not good enough and nothing I do works. Nothing has changed, and I feel hopeless. Any suggestions or ideas?
response_text:
It sounds like you're pouring everything you have into every part of your life—your relationships, your studies, your values—and yet the message you keep receiving is that it's still not enough. That's exhausting, and it makes complete sense that you feel worn out and hopeless right now.

I want to gently offer this: the fact that nothing you do seems to satisfy these voices might say more about *them* than about you. Some standards are impossible to meet no matter how hard we try, and constantly chasing someone else's approval can leave you empty. You've described a person who is genuinely trying, growing, and caring—that *is* enough. Consider whose voice is telling you otherwise, and whether it deserves that power over your worth. It may help to talk with a counselor who can support you in setting boundaries and building a sense of value that doesn't depend on others' approval. You deserve rest, and you deserve to feel proud of yourself.

prompt: It's been almost a year since my ex-boyfriend broke up with me after he cheated on me many times. I had found out about a month before, but I hadn't told him I knew because I didn't want us to break up. I used to have very low self-esteem, and I think it might have to do with my dad being an alcoholic. My father cheated on my mother when I was little. I wonder if this pain has to do with that. My ex-boyfriend and I were only dating for five months, but I still can't get over this betrayal. I'm not sure what to feel to get over it: forgiveness? Hate? He helped me financially after our break up by lending me $3000, so I'm grateful for that. I still hate him for what he did and still want him to like me although we're not even talking anymore. We follow each other on Instagram and that's it. I feel like I still need his validation. This is haunting me day and night. I want to focus on my new relationship and goals, but I keep obsessing over this and keep checking my ex-boyfriend's Instagram and Facebook. I feel so bad and keep having nightmares.
response_text:
Thank you for sharing something so painful and personal. What you're feeling makes complete sense. When someone betrays us, especially in ways that echo earlier wounds—like your father's cheating—it can hit far deeper than the length of the relationship might suggest. You're not just grieving five months; you may be grieving a lifelong pattern of feeling like love comes with betrayal.

It's also normal to feel tangled emotions—hatred, gratitude, longing for his validation—all at once. These don't cancel each other out. But wanting him to like you likely isn't really about him; it's about wanting proof that you're worthy of love. You already are, regardless of what he thinks.

Checking his social media keeps reopening the wound. Consider muting or unfollowing him—not out of hate, but to protect your healing. And given how much this connects to your past, working with a therapist could help you untangle these deeper roots. You deserve peace, and it's absolutely possible to find it.

prompt: I'm a male in my 20s. My girlfriend is in her late 30s. She's great. She's funny and smart, she has a big heart, and we have an excellent sex life. She recently moved in with me partially because she wanted to and partially because she had no place to go. We fight a lot. It’s mostly my fault, I must admit. She doesn't like my insecurity and lack of trust I have for her. I have trust issues. Also, I can't fathom why a woman like her is with me, so I'm always dreading when a better dude will come along. I don't think she's happy. She's very submissive and she loves me very much, but also the fact that she has nowhere to go must be influencing her decision to stay. She has no place to go so I feel like I can’t break up with her. I’m literally trapped.
response_text:
It sounds like you love her deeply, and that love is getting tangled up with fear—fear that you're not enough, that she'll leave, that you're somehow keeping her trapped. Those are heavy feelings to carry, and I can hear how much you want to do right by her.

Here's something worth considering: your insecurity and jealousy aren't permanent facts about you. They're patterns that can be worked on, often with a therapist's help. Ending the relationship to "set her free" might feel noble, but it could also be a way of avoiding the harder work of examining where those trust issues come from.

Before making a big decision, try talking with her honestly—not "should we break up," but "here's what I'm struggling with, and I want to be better for us." Let her have a voice in this too. She's an adult who can decide what she wants. And if leaving is ever right, help her find footing rather than making that choice for her.

prompt: About 3 years ago or so I was skinny, but I was still ugly. I really do want to change that but I've tried 3 times. Now can I try but don't stop. At school I get bullied about my weight and my ugliness and I have been bullied my whole life that I believe them. How can I stop thinking about them and don't let it get in my head? response_text:
I can hear how much pain you're carrying, and I want you to know that being bullied for years is not okay—and it says nothing about your worth. When people hear cruel things every day, it makes sense they start to believe them. But those bullies are wrong about you, even when it feels true.

It took real courage to ask your parents for a therapist. Sometimes parents don't fully understand, but that doesn't mean your feelings aren't valid. Could you try telling them specifically how much this hurts—maybe in a letter if talking feels hard? You could also reach out to a school counselor, teacher, or trusted adult who might help you get support.

Please know your body doesn't determine your value, and you deserve to feel safe. If these thoughts ever get overwhelming, you can text a crisis line (like 741741 in the US) anytime. You reached out here—that matters. Keep reaching out. You're not alone in this.

prompt: Everyone around me is much smarter and flaunts it. Everyone around me is skinny, and here I am trying to throw up so I'm not fat. Everything I do is wrong, and I can't seem to do anything right! No one else at school seems to feel the way I do! Is this normal teenage girls feelings? I don't think these feelings are normal.
response_text:
It takes real courage to put these feelings into words, and I'm glad you did. What you're describing sounds incredibly painful—feeling like you don't measure up, like everything's wrong. Please know those feelings are valid, even if they're not the whole truth about who you are.

I do want to gently name something: making yourself throw up to control your weight is a sign that you're hurting more than a person should have to carry alone. That part isn't something to just push through by yourself. Please tell a trusted adult—a parent, counselor, or doctor—so you can get real support.
