Many teens feel insecure and compare themselves to others, so you're not alone in that. But you deserve care for what you're going through, not just to tough it out. You matter, and reaching out here shows you already know you're worth helping.

prompt: These "jokes" are made about everything. They seem to have the need to say something "funny" about everything. It's not funny, just awkward.
response_text:
It sounds like you're dealing with someone whose constant joking has become genuinely draining rather than entertaining. That kind of humor—where there's a quip about everything—can feel exhausting, and it makes sense that you're frustrated. Sometimes people use jokes as a shield or a habit, but that doesn't mean you have to keep absorbing the awkwardness in silence.

If this is someone you interact with regularly, it might help to gently name what you're feeling in the moment—something like, "I'd actually like to just talk about this seriously." You're allowed to set that boundary, and you're allowed to not laugh when something isn't funny to you. If it keeps bothering you, it may be worth reflecting on how much space this person's behavior takes up in your life and whether you want to address it more directly.

prompt: It's really hard to not have negative feelings about friends who don't put any effort into nourishing our relationship.
response_text:
It makes complete sense that you'd feel this way. When you're consistently the one reaching out, initiating plans, or checking in, it can leave you feeling undervalued and even a little lonely—like the care you offer isn't being returned. Those negative feelings aren't a flaw in you; they're a signal that something in the relationship feels unbalanced, and that your needs matter.

It might help to gently ask yourself what you're hoping for from these friendships, and whether it's worth naming the imbalance to the people involved. Sometimes friends don't realize how one-sided things have become, and an honest conversation can shift things. Other times, it may mean adjusting your own expectations to protect your energy. Either way, you deserve relationships where effort flows both ways—and it's okay to prioritize the ones that do.

prompt: I was “mentored” by this guy for a few years spiritually. It was okay at times, but other times, it was just weird. I try not to think about it too much, but a lot of manipulation and lying happened, yet no one else really believed me when I told them. It's like he's two different people, and no one else really sees that side of him. I was blamed for a lot of our troubles, and now we don't really talk much. I'm worried because he's in a trusted position of leadership and no one suspects anything. They just think I'm attacking his character. How do I know for sure?
response_text:
It sounds like you've been carrying something heavy and lonely—not only the experience itself, but the pain of not being believed. That's a real and understandable burden, and I want you to know your perception of what happened matters, even when others don't validate it.

The doubt you're feeling ("How do I know for sure?") is actually common for people who've experienced manipulation—it can leave you second-guessing your own reality. One thing that can help is writing down specific events as you remember them: what was said, done, and how it affected you. Seeing patterns on paper can clarify things and ground you in your own experience. It might also help to talk with a therapist who understands spiritual abuse and manipulation dynamics; they can offer perspective without the bias others in that community may have.

You don't have to solve the question of exposing him all at once. Right now, focus on your own healing and trusting yourself again. That's a valid and important place to start.

prompt: I would like to be able to have more positive relationships in the present.
response_text:
It sounds like you're recognizing something important—that connection and positive relationships matter to you, and you want to nurture them starting now. That awareness is a meaningful first step.

Building more positive relationships often begins with small, intentional actions: reaching out to someone you care about, being present and genuinely listening when you're with others, and allowing yourself to be a little vulnerable and open. It can also help to reflect on what "positive" means to you—whether it's more honesty, more warmth, or feeling truly seen. If past experiences have made relationships feel difficult, be patient and compassionate with yourself as you try new approaches. Meaningful connection grows gradually. Consider starting with one relationship you'd like to strengthen, and notice what small step you could take this week. If you find deeper patterns getting in the way, talking with a therapist could offer valuable support. You clearly care about the people in your life, and that intention is a strong foundation to build on.

prompt: They're calling me names like hypocrite and a baby even when they act in the same manner as I do. I'm tired of being called names. What should I do?
response_text:
Being called names—especially when the other person acts the same way—is genuinely frustrating and hurtful. It makes sense that you're feeling worn down by it. You deserve to be treated with respect, regardless of who's "right" in any given moment.

One thing that can help is separating their words from your worth. When someone calls you a hypocrite or a baby, that often says more about their own frustration or defensiveness than it does about you. You don't have to accept those labels as truth. If it feels safe, you might calmly set a boundary—something like, "I'm not okay with being called names, and I'd like us to talk without that." If they keep doing it, giving yourself permission to step away from those conversations is a valid form of self-protection. Who are these people to you, and how much space do they take up in your life? That might help you decide how much energy this is worth.

prompt: My brother has been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia and has not been taking his medication. He's been using methamphetamine and alcohol and was found sleeping naked in my step mom driveway in 12 degree weather. I was adopted in by his dad (who just passed) and his mother will not Get involved because she's afraid of financial responsibility. Do I have the rights to be able to sign my brother into mentalhealth facility?
response_text:
I'm so sorry you're carrying this heavy situation, especially while grieving your father's recent passing. Watching your brother in this kind of danger—sleeping naked in freezing weather, using substances, off his medication—is frightening, and it says a lot about your love that you're searching for ways to help.

The ability to have someone involuntarily committed varies by state, and usually requires that the person is an immediate danger to themselves or others. In many places, you don't need to be a legal guardian to initiate this—you can call for an emergency psychiatric evaluation, and a crisis team, doctor, or judge makes the decision. Given the freezing exposure and substance use, this may qualify. I'd encourage you to contact a local mental health crisis line or call 911 during an emergency, and ask about "emergency psychiatric hold" laws where you live.

You don't have to figure this out alone. Please reach out to a crisis resource today—your brother's safety may depend on it.

prompt: I'm a female in my mid 20s. Lately I tend to over drink and I've become a very angry drunk. In the past, I have even cheated on my boyfriend while I was under the influence of alcohol. But now, even if I don't do anything wrong and don't embarrass myself, I still feel really guilty after a night of drinking. I don't understand why I'm feeling this way. Does this mean I have a problem?
response_text:
Thank you for being so honest—that takes real courage, especially when you're carrying guilt. What you're describing does sound worth paying attention to. Drinking to the point of anger, blackouts, or actions you regret, and feeling persistent guilt afterward even when nothing "bad" happened, are signs that alcohol may be affecting you more than you'd like. That guilt might be your mind's way of signaling that something feels out of alignment with your values.

This doesn't have to mean you're broken or beyond help—it means you're noticing a pattern, and noticing is the first step toward change. It might help to talk with a doctor or counselor who can explore your relationship with alcohol without judgment. You could also try tracking how much and why you drink, and what emotions come up around it. You deserve support in understanding this, and you don't have to figure it out alone. Reaching out, like you just did, is a meaningful start.

prompt: Or how to send him somewhere that can help him, something like The Baker Act.
response_text:
It sounds like you're really worried about someone you care about and trying to figure out how to get them help—that's a caring and difficult position to be in.

The Baker Act (in Florida) allows for involuntary examination if someone is a danger to themselves or others, or is severely unable to care for themselves due to mental illness. To initiate it, you can call 911 or your local police, who can assess the situation, or contact a mental health professional or a judge to request an evaluation. Other states have similar laws, sometimes called "civil commitment" or a "72-hour hold."

If your loved one is in immediate danger, please call 911 or the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988) right away. They can guide you through the next steps.

Would you feel comfortable sharing a bit more about what's happening with him? Knowing whether it's an emergency versus ongoing concern would help point you toward the right kind of support.

prompt: I have bipolar II disorder, I'm addicted to alcohol and weed, and I'm hopeless. I keep drinking even though it's harming myself and others.
response_text:
It takes real courage to name all of this so honestly. Bipolar II, addiction, and hopelessness together is an incredibly heavy load to carry, and the fact that you can see how the drinking is affecting you and others—even while feeling stuck—shows more self-awareness and strength than you may be giving yourself credit for.

Hopelessness lies to us; it tells us nothing can change when it actually can, especially with the right support. Because bipolar and substance use feed into each other, treating them together tends to work best. If you can, reaching out to a doctor or a dual-diagnosis program could be a real turning point—you don't have to untangle this alone.

If you ever feel unsafe or like you might harm yourself, please reach out right away by calling or texting 988 (in the US). You reached out here, and that matters. Please keep reaching out—you're worth the effort it takes to heal.

prompt: My new daughter-in-law just informed me that she is smoking marijuana while pregnant because of her morning sickness. I’m in shock and I don’t know how to respond. I just lost my mom, and she was good with advice.
response_text:
I'm so sorry for the loss of your mom—grieving while facing a worry like this makes everything harder, and it's understandable you feel shaken.

It's natural to be concerned, and your instinct to protect your future grandchild comes from love. When you're ready to talk with your daughter-in-law, try leading with care rather than alarm—something like, "I can see you're really suffering with the nausea. I worry about you and the baby, and I'd love to help you find some relief that feels safe." Gently encouraging her to talk with her doctor about her symptoms and options can open the door without her feeling judged. Doctors can suggest alternatives and give her accurate information she may trust more than any of us.

You can't control her choices, but you can stay a steady, loving presence—which is often what keeps that door open. Be gentle with yourself too; you're carrying grief and worry at once.

prompt: I am a survivor of multiple sexual abuse/rape experiences. Triggers are having an effect on my daily life and my sexual relationship with my partner. I'm trying to learn to cope with them.
response_text:
Thank you for sharing something so deeply personal—it takes real courage to speak about these experiences and to actively seek ways to heal. Surviving multiple traumas and continuing to move forward each day shows tremendous strength, even when it doesn't feel that way. It makes complete sense that triggers are affecting your daily life and intimacy; your mind and body are responding to protect you, and that's not a failing on your part.

Learning to cope is a gradual process, and you don't have to do it alone. If you haven't already, working with a therapist who specializes in trauma—particularly approaches like EMDR or trauma-focused therapy—can be genuinely helpful. It may also support your relationship to gently share with your partner what feels safe and what doesn't, perhaps with a couples or sex therapist guiding those conversations. Please be patient and compassionate with yourself along the way. Healing isn't linear, and every small step you take matters. You deserve support and safety.

prompt: I recently lost a friend to suicide. I'm smoking marijuana and drinking more to cope with it. How can I handle this better?
response_text:
I'm so sorry for the loss of your friend. Losing someone to suicide brings a uniquely painful mix of grief—sadness, confusion, guilt, even anger—and it makes complete sense that you're looking for ways to numb it. Please know that turning to substances during pain like this is a very human response, and you're not a failure for it.

The tricky part is that alcohol and marijuana tend to delay grief rather than ease it, and they can deepen low moods over time. You don't have to white-knuckle through this alone, though. Consider reaching out to a grief counselor or a support group specifically for suicide loss survivors—organizations like the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention have resources for exactly this. Leaning on trusted people, gentle movement, and letting yourself actually feel the grief in small doses can help more than avoiding it.

If you ever feel overwhelmed or unsafe, please reach out to a crisis line (call or text 988 in the US). You deserve support through this.

prompt: I have been diagnosed with posttraumatic stress disorder due to my military experiences. Not a year ago, I had a car accident. Could this experience add more problems?
response_text:
Thank you for your service, and for reaching out about this. It's a very understandable concern.

Yes, a car accident can potentially compound existing PTSD, especially since it may share features with combat-related trauma—sudden danger, loss of control, threat to life. Sometimes a new traumatic event can reactivate old symptoms or add new ones, like anxiety while driving or fresh intrusive memories. But this isn't guaranteed, and having a diagnosis doesn't mean you're destined to get worse.

The most helpful step is to talk with your mental health provider about the accident specifically. They can assess whether it's affected your symptoms and adjust your treatment if needed. Trauma-focused therapies like CPT or EMDR are effective for both military and accident-related trauma, so support is available regardless.

If you notice new symptoms—more nightmares, avoidance, jumpiness, or trouble driving—please mention them without minimizing. You've already shown strength by seeking answers. You don't have to navigate this alone.

prompt: How can I get therapy for posttraumatic stress disorder without any money or insurance?
response_text:
Accessing PTSD treatment without money or insurance is challenging, but there are real options worth pursuing.

Start by looking into community mental health centers, which often offer sliding-scale fees based on income or free services. If you're in the US, you can call 211 or visit 211.org to find local low-cost resources. University training clinics (where supervised graduate students provide therapy) are another affordable option and often have openings. If you're a veteran, the VA provides PTSD care. Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) also offer care regardless of ability to pay.

For immediate support, Open Path Collective connects people with therapists for reduced rates, and warmlines (non-crisis peer support phone lines) can help between sessions. Apps like PTSD Coach, developed by the VA, are free and evidence-informed.

Reaching out for help while carrying this weight takes real courage, and you deserve support. Consider starting with one call this week—even a single step forward matters. You don't have to navigate this alone.

prompt: As a child, my parents injured my brother, so they went to prison. I was there when he had gotten hurt, but I can't seem to remember. I also can't remember being with them quite well. It's a blur.
response_text:
What you're describing—the blurriness, the missing memories—makes a lot of sense given what you went through. When we experience something frightening or overwhelming as children, especially involving the people who were supposed to protect us, our minds sometimes protect us by blocking out those memories. This is a common response to trauma, not a flaw in you or a sign that something's wrong with your memory.

You don't have to force yourself to remember, and you don't owe anyone those details. What matters is how you're feeling now, carrying all of this. If you're open to it, working with a trauma-informed therapist could help you gently make sense of what happened at a pace that feels safe for you. You went through something no child should have to, and it's okay to give yourself compassion as you continue to process it.

prompt: I'm a teenager, and I just got my first job. I am a month and a half in. Yesterday, my boss pushed me to the point where I had to go to the restroom and cry. She didn't see me, and I'm glad, but when I went to talk to her about it today, I let a tear or two come out. I hate it. I feel like they're not going to keep me anymore.
response_text:
First, congratulations on landing your first job—that's a real accomplishment, and the fact that you're already advocating for yourself by talking to your boss shows maturity most adults struggle with.

Crying doesn't make you weak or unprofessional; it means you care and you're human. Bosses have seen tears before, and a tear or two while addressing something difficult isn't grounds for letting someone go. What matters more is that you showed up, faced the situation, and communicated. That takes courage.

It might help to reflect on what specifically pushed you to that point yesterday—was it the workload, the way she spoke to you, or something else? Understanding that can help you decide how to handle it next time. You're new, and learning to manage stress at work is part of the process for everyone. Be gentle with yourself. One hard day doesn't define your worth as an employee or a person.

prompt: My wife is always accusing me of cheating and telling me that I'm doing things she finds disrespectful even when I don't mean it like that. For example, she gets offended when I call someone at work "sweetheart." I wish I had a penny for every time she accused me of cheating on her. She doesn't, and never will say she was wrong. How do I get her to understand?
response_text:
It sounds exhausting to feel constantly accused and misunderstood, especially when you're trying to act in good faith. That kind of ongoing tension can wear down even a strong relationship.

One thing worth considering is that her reactions—while frustrating—may be coming from a place of insecurity or past hurt rather than a desire to control you. That doesn't make the accusations fair, but it might open the door to a different kind of conversation. Instead of trying to get her to admit she's wrong, which often just deepens defensiveness on both sides, you might try asking what's underneath the fear. Something like, "I want you to feel secure with me—can you help me understand what worries you?" can shift things from blame toward teamwork.

If these patterns keep repeating despite your efforts, couples counseling could give you both a neutral space to be heard. You deserve to feel trusted, and she deserves to feel safe—those goals aren't in conflict.

prompt: I am in a high stress position for a tech company. I am being overworked and underpaid for my contributions and it is not only giving me anxiety, but also demoralizing. What can I do to manage my stress?
response_text:
That sounds genuinely exhausting—feeling both overworked and undervalued can wear down even the most resilient person, and it makes sense that your anxiety and motivation are suffering.

In the short term, look for small ways to protect your energy: set clearer boundaries around your working hours, take real breaks during the day, and try to disconnect fully when you're off. Physical movement, decent sleep, and time with people who fill your cup can genuinely buffer stress. But it's also worth stepping back and asking a bigger question—is this situation something that can realistically change, or is your body telling you it's time to explore other options? Documenting your contributions could help you make a case for better pay, or serve as a portfolio if you decide to look elsewhere.

You deserve to be compensated and respected for your work. Managing the stress matters, but don't lose sight of the fact that the source of it may need addressing too. Be gentle with yourself here.

prompt: I've worked with this guy for about three years now, and I knew the first time I saw him that I was attracted. Over time, he became a very dear friend, and we talked about our relationship problems, family, dreams, and so on. There was always flirtation with us, and one day pretty recently, it progressed to making out. We agreed to keep it quiet, and we did, but in the back of my mind, I hoped it would become something more. It didn't, and three months later, I'm still not over it. I'm trying so hard to maintain the friendship because that's what he wants. We're no longer in the same office, which I thought would help me get over these feelings, but we still talk about work, and he's constantly touching me, so I'm still very drawn to him. He's a hugger and such a sweet guy, so I find myself fantasizing all the time about what could have been and what could still be, but he's clearly not interested. He's younger than me and prefers model types, but I see him checking me out a lot, which gives me hope. How do I get him out of my system and still maintain the friendship?
response_text:
It sounds like you're caught in a really painful loop—hoping for more while trying to protect a friendship that keeps reopening the wound. The mixed signals (his touching, the checking-out) make it even harder, because they feed the hope that keeps you stuck.

Here's the honest thing: it may not be possible to "get him out of your system" while you're still in this much contact and physical closeness. Every hug and lingering look resets your feelings. If you truly want to heal, you might need to create real distance for a while—fewer chats, no physical affection, maybe naming a boundary like "I need some space to reset." That's not abandoning the friendship; it's giving yourself a chance to grieve what didn't happen so a genuine friendship could eventually exist.

Try to gently notice when you're fantasizing and bring yourself back to reality: he told you what he wants. You deserve someone who chooses you fully. Be as kind to yourself in this as you'd be to a friend.
